newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU urged to boost wheat refund to foil Argentina.
newsitem.headline: EU urged to boost wheat refund to foil Argentina.

text.p: European wheat exporters, fearful of losing markets to cheaper Argentine supplies, want the EU to grant higher export subsidies through its weekly grain tender system, industry sources said on Wednesday.
But Brussels is more concerned about avoiding a subsidy war with the U.S. and has so far ignored their demands, which would lead to the EU undercutting U.S. prices.
Lower internal grain prices in the EU and a stronger dollar point to a lower EU refund for wheat this week if the idea is to match U.S. prices, traders and analysts have said.
The EU restricted wheat and barley exports through export taxes last year, but has restored refunds to bridge the gap between local prices and what are now lower prices in the U.S.
In a bid to avoid possible conflict over subsidies with Washington, Brussels has promised to match but not undercut U.S. wheat with its export refunds.
Last week the EU granted 192,450 tonnes of wheat from the open market at a subsidy of 6.49 Ecus per tonne, making the sale worth $170-$185 per tonne, FOB, depending on quality and origin.
Taking into account freight costs, Argentine new crop wheat is currently at $145 per tonne on world markets.
Some exporters, eager to cover import demand from North African countries such as Algeria, Morocco and Egypt, said they would like the EU to raise its refund by two to three Ecus.
They also argued a higher refund was needed if the EU wanted to avoid losing sales in markets such as Iran, Iraq and Eastern Europe.
"Brussels must be more generous. This could help cover current business destined to the Mediterranean region," one said.
"The United States forced the EU to follow the U.S. market. But this cannot work," another exporter said.
The U.S. has hinted that current EU wheat refunds are not high enough to spark a subsidy war. But it has threatened to use its own subsidies if necessary to meet aggressive EU competition.
Traders said the EU had less than three months to step up wheat exports before a bumper Argentine crop became available.
Traders estimated EU wheat export commitments currently accounted for 16 percent of potential exports of 15.5-17.5 million tonnes (including food aid and products) for 1996/97.
U.S. export commitments stand at 75 percent of the year's potential, Argentine commitments at 18 percent and Australian commitments at 20 percent, they said.
Internal EU wheat prices have eased in recent weeks under pressure from a bumper 90 million tonne harvest.
But the EU Commission, eager to keep its wheat subsidies as low as possible, has said prices are still too high.
In France ex-farm wheat is currently about six percent above EU-guaranteed intervention support prices.
